name: Isfahan
info: Isfahan is a city in central Iran on the Zayandeh River, a regional centre under the Medes and a capital under the Parthians, Seljuks and Safavids, best known for the square and boulevard of Abbas the Great.

facts.founded: No founding date is given: the area was inhabited from the Palaeolithic, the site became a regional centre under the Medes, and a diverse city is recorded under Cyrus the Great, whose edict of 538 BCE is the first date connected with it.
facts.where: On the plain of the Zayandeh River at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 440 kilometres south of Tehran, in Isfahan Province, Iran.
facts.known: The Seljuk capital under Malik-Shah I; Timur's massacre of 1387; Abbas the Great's capital from 1598; Naqsh-e Jahan Square and the Chahar Bagh boulevard; the bridges over the Zayandeh; New Julfa and its Armenians; the proverb 'Isfahan is half the world'
facts.today: Isfahan is the capital of Isfahan Province and the third most populous city in Iran, with a population of about 2,238,000.

t: Isfahan was a regional centre under the Medes and a city of mixed peoples under the Achaemenids, and it grew under the Buyids and the Seljuks, whose ruler Toghril Beg made it his capital in the mid-11th century.

Timur's army killed, reportedly, 70,000 of its people in 1387, but in 1598 Abbas the Great made it the Safavid capital and rebuilt it round a new square and a boulevard, settling craftsmen and Armenians there by force.
After Central Asian invaders sacked it in 1722 it declined, and the capital moved to Mashhad, then to Shiraz, and in 1775 to Tehran.
dyk: Timur's soldiers reportedly killed 70,000 people in Isfahan in 1387, and an eyewitness counted more than 28 towers, each built of about 1,500 heads.

sections.origins:
Human habitation in the Isfahan region can be traced back to the Palaeolithic period, and archaeologists have found artefacts of the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Bronze and Iron ages. Under Median rule the commercial entrepôt began to show signs of settled urban life and grew into a regional centre, helped by the fertile soil on the banks of the Zayandeh River, in a region called Aspandana or Ispandana.

When Cyrus the Great joined Persian and Median lands in the Achaemenid Empire, the city was already religiously and ethnically diverse and became an early example of the king's reputed religious tolerance. In 538 BCE, after taking Babylon, Cyrus made an edict allowing the Jews of Babylon to return to Jerusalem, and some of those who emigrated settled in Isfahan instead. The 10th-century historian Ibn al-Faqih wrote that Jews fleeing Nebuchadnezzar carried a sample of the water and soil of Jerusalem and settled where the soil and water were thought to resemble it, in a place called Yahudia.

The name Ispahan comes from the Middle Persian Spahān, found on seals and inscriptions including that of the Zoroastrian magus Kartir. Ptolemy gives it as Aspadana or Aspazana, which means 'place of gathering for the army', and the name is believed to come from the Old Persian plural spādānām, 'the armies'. Other ancient names were Gey, Jey, Partakān, Park and Judea. The Zoroastrian city had the Parthian and Achaemenid name Gabae, shortened under the Sasanians to Gay, on the northern bank of the Zayandeh.
sections.growth:
After the Arab capture of 642, Isfahan grew prosperous under the Buyids, and its walls are thought to date from the 10th century. Toghril Beg, the Turkish founder of the Seljuk dynasty, made it his capital in the mid-11th century, and it grew in size and splendour under his grandson Malik-Shah I, who reigned from 1073 to 1092. Benjamin of Tudela reported 15,000 Jews in the city in 1170. After the Seljuks fell, about 1200, Isfahan temporarily declined and was eclipsed by Tabriz and Qazvin. During his visit in 1327 Ibn Battuta noted that it was one of the largest and fairest of cities but in ruins for the greater part.

The city's second golden age began in 1598, when Abbas the Great moved his capital from Qazvin to the more central Isfahan and rebuilt it as one of the largest cities of the 17th century. He pursued policies to increase Iranian involvement in the Silk Road trade. The plan added the rectangular Shah Square and the straight Chahar Bagh boulevard, with a large garden, now the gardens of Hasht Behesht, between them. A turquoise gate joined the square to the Grand Bazaar and the old square, and the Shah Mosque on the south side became the main place of worship.

Sheikh Baha'i, an engineer of Abbas, designed a network of canals called madi that carried water from the Zayandeh to different parts of the city: 77 on the northern course of the river and 71 on the southern. The Allahverdi Khan Bridge, Si-o-se-pol, 295 metres long, joined the city to New Julfa. Shah Abbas II built the Khaju Bridge in 1650. Jean Chardin wrote that there were 273 baths in Safavid Isfahan.
sections.rulers:
Under the Medes the site was a regional centre. The Achaemenids ruled it from the time of Cyrus the Great, and under the Parthians, who held power from 247 BCE to 224 CE, Arsacid governors administered the provinces from Isfahan, whose urban development quickened to suit a capital. In the Sasanian era, from 224 to 651 CE, a group called the Espoohrans, descended from seven noble Iranian families, governed the city. Its political importance declined, but its military role grew, and Sasanian princes studied statecraft there. Its position at the crossing of the roads to Susa and Persepolis made it a base for a standing army.

The Arabs captured Isfahan in 642 and made it the capital of al-Jabal province, much of ancient Media. The Persian Buyid dynasty, which came to rule much of Iran as Abbasid authority waned in the 10th century, was followed by the Seljuks under Toghril Beg and Malik-Shah I. Isfahan surrendered to Timur in 1387. The Safavids held power from 1501 to 1736, and Abbas the Great, who reigned from 1588 to 1629, made it his capital in 1598, the second time in its history that it had been the capital of Iran.

After the Safavids the capital moved to Mashhad under the Afsharids, then to Shiraz under the Zand, and in 1775 to Tehran, by Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, founder of the Qajar dynasty. Early in the 19th century Mohammad Hossein Khan began to preserve some of Isfahan's archaeologically important buildings, in the reign of Fath-Ali Shah Qajar.
sections.life:
Isfahan was home to many peoples. Under Cyrus it was religiously and ethnically diverse, and under the Parthians tolerance continued. Queen Shushandukht, the Jewish wife of Yazdegerd I (reigned 399 to 420) and mother of Bahram V, is said to have settled a colony of Jews at Yahudiyyeh, about 3 kilometres from the Zoroastrian city, and after the Arab conquest the population of Gay shrank while that of Yahudiyyeh and its suburbs grew, forming the nucleus of the later city.

Abbas the Great forcibly resettled Turkish, Armenian and Persian craftsmen in the city to ensure its prosperity. As many as 300,000 Armenians, mostly from Jugha, were forcibly resettled, and some were brought to Isfahan, where he ordered a new quarter for them, New Julfa, named from Old Julfa. Most of its churches stand there, among them St Jakob (1607), St Mary (1613), Bedkhem (1627) and Vank Cathedral (1664), and Pacifique de Provins founded a French mission in the city in 1627. The royal court held many Georgian military servants and women, and the city had enclaves of Georgian, Circassian and Daghestani descent, estimated at 20,000 by Engelbert Kaempfer, who was in Iran in 1684 and 1685.

Opium dens and coffeehouses around the Chahar Bagh and the Chehel Sotoun served as social hubs, and the Isfahan School of painting flourished in the Safavid era. Isfahan became known in Europe, and travellers such as Jean Chardin described it. The Esfahani dialect is one of the main dialects of Western Persian, and the city's Jewish districts speak a distinct dialect.
sections.crises:
In 1387 Isfahan surrendered to Timur and was at first treated with relative mercy. The city then revolted against his punitive taxes, killing the tax collectors and some of his soldiers. In retribution Timur ordered a massacre of the residents, and his soldiers reportedly killed 70,000 citizens. An eyewitness counted more than 28 towers, each built of about 1,500 heads.

The city had already declined after the fall of the Seljuks about 1200, and Ibn Battuta saw much of it in ruins in 1327. In 1722, during a marked decline in Safavid influence, Central Asian invaders sacked Isfahan. Afterwards the city lost importance, and the capital moved away, first to Mashhad and then to Shiraz and Tehran.

In the 20th century people from southern Iran settled in Isfahan, many during the migrations early in the century and in the 1980s after the Iran–Iraq War, in which 23,000 people from Isfahan were killed and there were 43,000 veterans. During the Second World War Polish refugees, mostly children, were admitted to the city, with 21 childcare units and some 2,600 Poles housed there in February 1943, before they were evacuated to Africa, India and New Zealand.
sections.legacy:
The fame of Isfahan produced the Persian proverb Esfahān nesf-e-jahān ast, 'Isfahan is half the world'. Naqsh-e Jahan Square, also called Shah Square or Imam Square, is among the largest city squares in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The city centre has an older section round the Jameh Mosque and the Safavid expansion round the square, with palaces, bazaars and places of worship nearby, among them the Ali Qapu, Chehel Sotoun and Hasht Behesht palaces. The Grand Bazaar and its Qeysarie Gate were built in the 17th century.

Isfahan is known for the Isfahan rug, usually of merino wool and silk, and the city still produces carpets, textiles, steel, handicrafts and traditional sweets. It also keeps ancient festivals such as Tirgan and Sepandārmazgān, and theatre performances began there in 1919. The Armenian quarter of New Julfa is today one of the largest Armenian quarters in the world.

The city is the capital of Isfahan Province and the third most populous city in Iran, after Tehran and Mashhad, with approximately 2,238,000 people, and lies 440 kilometres south of Tehran. It stands where the two principal routes across Iran, north to south and east to west, meet.

summary: Isfahan, in central Iran, was a regional centre under the Medes and a capital under the Seljuks and, from 1598, the Safavids, when Abbas the Great rebuilt it round a new square and boulevard. Timur's massacre of 1387 and a sack in 1722 marked its setbacks, and it remains one of Iran's largest cities.
notes: No founding date is given by the article. I used -538 (circa) as 'start' because Cyrus's edict of 538 BCE is the earliest date it attaches to the city; this is a convention, not a foundation date. The editor may prefer a different start or null.

The task asked for 'the Afghan siege of 1722'. The article says only: 'The city was sacked by Central Asian invaders in 1722, during a marked decline in Safavid influence.' It does not say Afghan, siege, or give figures, so I wrote 'sacked by Central Asian invaders' and no more. A second source is needed for the Hotak Afghans and the siege.

Timur 1387: the article says 'reportedly killing 70,000' and 'an eyewitness counted more than 28 towers, each constructed of about 1,500 heads'. It names no source for either. 28 x 1,500 is about 42,000 heads, below 70,000; I did not reconcile them.

Parthian-era dates are 247 BCE to 224 CE for the dynasty (as the article gives); the article says the city served as the Arsacid governors' base but gives no date for this. The Sasanian era is 224 to 651 CE.

The article's account of the Jewish colony is inconsistent: it attributes the colony to Nebuchadnezzar's time (the Ibn al-Faqih passage), to the Achaemenid return from Babylon, and to Queen Shushandukht (late 4th and early 5th century), and says the Nebuchadnezzar attribution 'is unlikely'. I gave all three as the article gives them, with their attributions.

The article says Isfahan became capital of Iran 'for the second time in its history' under Abbas but does not say when the first was; I kept the phrase without specifying (the Seljuk capital is a likely first but the article does not say so for all Iran).

The 'Khwarazmian and Mongol era' section of the article is empty: nothing could be said of the Mongol period or of Khwarazmian rule. 'Muslim conquest' puts the Arab capture in 642; the section on the Safavids gives Abbas's reign as 1588 to 1629. The Esfahani dialect, qualified 'one of the main dialects', is the article's.

Left out: the present government's measures (loudspeakers, surveillance, protests, nuclear and military facilities), the economy and tourism, the article's lists of schools, mosques and sports; I did not describe the 2018 farmers' protest. The 'Armenians' figure of 300,000 refers to those resettled in total, only some of whom came to Isfahan; the article gives no number for New Julfa.
The article contains a sentence saying New Julfa is 'one of the largest Armenian quarters in the world' today; I kept it with 'today'.
